To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dry plant biomass, detached from plants, and structural plant components emit significant amounts of the greenhouse gas methane upon irradiation and/or heating, that this process is photochemically driven, and that this process is not related to the biological activity of the plant.
dry plant material, and in particular the cuticle, emits methane when irradiated with UV light and that heating can also induce emissions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plant material and living plants emit methane under certain conditions.
CH4 emissions from plant biomass and plant structural components are real, significant and not due to artifacts.
UV irradiation of plant material, as it occurs in natural ecosystems, is the main source for CH4 production from plants and plant biomass.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CH4 is produced by photochemical processes from the plant material and structural components and is emitted from the plant surface, but not from the plant itself.

CH4 is produced by photochemical reactions in the presence of UV light, that this photochemical process is independent from the carbon isotope ratio of the substrate, and that CH4 is stored in a large reservoir in the plant material.
the emission of methane upon irradiating plant material with UV light is real and that the process is not an artifact of the experimental set-up.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emission of CH4 from plant material is not an artifact, but a genuine process that is likely to be of importance for the global budget of this greenhouse gas.
the reported CH4 emissions from living plants and plant material do not represent artifacts or interferences, and that the emission process is not limited to living plants.
CH4 emissions from living plants and their structural components are not an artifact, but are caused by a photochemical process.
